idiom_name: instanceof with a type pattern: if (o instanceof Flushable f) f.flush()
implementation_notes: Java's capability query is a type test against an interface, and since the type pattern arrived (JEP 394, final in Java 16) the test and the handle are one expression: `if (o instanceof Flushable f) f.flush();` - no separate cast, and the pattern variable exists only where the compiler knows the test succeeded (Oracle's Pattern Matching with instanceof page shows the old test-then-cast pair it replaces). Interfaces are the capability unit; because a class may implement any number of them, the query never needs a cross-cast, and the negative answer is simply the else branch. The reflective Class.isInstance / Class.isAssignableFrom form remains justified when the capability type is only known at run time as a Class token - the JVM's runtime type record supports it, at the cost of reflection overhead.
pitfalls: Generic type arguments are erased: `o instanceof List<String>` is a compile-time error and a raw or wildcard test checks only the raw type - re-check element capabilities explicitly.
The pattern variable is in scope only on paths where the test is known true; combining the condition with || (or capturing the value in a lambda that outlives the branch) breaks that flow typing.

The test is nominal, so a proxy or decorator that forwards the methods but does not declare the interface answers false; declare the interface or negotiate a capability object instead of trusting a forwarding wrapper.
Reflection (isInstance, isAssignableFrom) bypasses the compile-time check and is markedly slower; confine it to framework boundaries.

variants.name: Runtime Class token (Class.isInstance / isAssignableFrom)
variants.implementation_notes: When the capability type is only known as data - a plugin descriptor names it, a registry holds Class<?> objects - the query runs on the token rather than in the syntax: `if (capability.isInstance(o)) capability.cast(o).flush();`, with isAssignableFrom answering the type-to-type form of the question. This is the documented use case for the Class API (libraries and reflection-based utilities where the compiler cannot name the target type), written in ordinary Java 8: Class<T> tokens plus Optional as the absence channel. Prefer the type pattern whenever the capability interface is a compile-time constant: it is checked, non-reflective and needs no Class object.
variants.idiom_name: Class<T> token with isInstance(o) and an Optional-returning lookup helper
pitfalls: Class.isAssignableFrom(null) throws NullPointerException while isInstance(null) returns false; the two are not interchangeable.
A Class token obtained from a different class loader is not the same runtime type, so isInstance can answer false for an object that does implement the interface.
Primitives are boxed by isInstance and always answer false for the wrapper test unless the wrapper class itself is asked for.
